objectives: Describe the rise of Ghana, Mali and Songhai
Explain the importance of Mansa Musa and Timbuktu
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify dates and rulers: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage (1324), the Songhai defeat (1591), approximate periods of Ghana (early second millennium), Mali (13th–15th century) and Songhai (15th–16th century), and the origin of the modern name Ghana.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: Camel caravans crossed the **Sahara** carrying goods between West Africa and North Africa. The Sahara trade carried **salt** (from desert mines) and cloth, copper and beads south, and **gold**, ivory, kola nuts and slaves north. Traders and rulers grew wealthy. Towns on the edge of the desert, such as Timbuktu and Gao, became great markets. The trade also spread Islam and the Arabic script.

blocks.title: Ghana, Mali and Songhai
blocks.md:
- **Ghana** (ancient Ghana, called Wagadu): grew rich from taxing the gold and salt trade, and was strong in the early centuries of the second millennium.
- **Mali**: rose in the 13th century; its great ruler **Mansa Musa** travelled on pilgrimage to Mecca in **1324**, with so much gold that people spoke of it for years.
- **Songhai**: strong in the 15th–16th centuries; its capital was **Gao**.

**Timbuktu** was a centre of trade and learning, with mosques, schools and libraries where scholars copied and studied books. Rulers used governors, soldiers, taxes and a system of provinces to hold the empires together. Farmers, herders, fishermen, blacksmiths and craftworkers supported them; Songhai was strengthened by a strong army and river canoes on the Niger.

blocks.title: Decline
blocks.md: Empires weakened because of **quarrels over succession**, **revolts** by conquered peoples, difficult distances to control, and **attacks** from outside. Songhai was defeated in **1591** by a Moroccan army with firearms at Tondibi. Later, new trade routes by sea to the coast of West Africa reduced the importance of the Sahara routes.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Ancient Ghana is not the same place as modern Ghana; the modern country took the name in 1957 to honour the older empire.
- The dates of these empires are approximate and historians differ.
- Wealth came from controlling trade and taxing it, not only from owning gold mines.

blocks.title: Example 1: caravan trade
blocks.statement: Name two goods carried south and two carried north on the Sahara routes.
steps: Salt, cloth, copper and beads came from the north.
Gold, ivory, kola nuts and slaves went north.
So salt and cloth south; gold and ivory north.
blocks.answer: South: salt, cloth. North: gold, ivory.

blocks.title: Example 2: why the empires were powerful
blocks.statement: Explain how a ruler of Ghana became rich without owning every gold mine.
steps: Traders had to pass through his lands.
He taxed the goods entering and leaving.
So he earned from the trade.
blocks.answer: By taxing the trade that passed through his empire.
